title: Best Friends Read the Same Books
author: Christopher Perrin
summary: Christopher Perrin uses etymology as the entry point for a meditation on what a college, a colleague, and genuine education actually are. Tracing collegere (to read together) through its Latin roots—collegium (college), legere (to read, to choose), intelligere (to choose among)—he argues that the original ideal of higher education was a gathering of like-minded learners reading the same books toward the same ends: inquiry, wisdom, and deep conversation. He illustrates this with parallel etymologies of 'liberal arts' (liberating through words and numbers) and 'assessment' (to sit beside, from adsedere), each revealing a richer pedagogical vision than contemporary practice usually assumes. At Oxford, students still say 'I am reading philosophy' rather than majoring in it—preserving the root meaning that genuine learning is active, chosen, and collegial. The article argues that etymology is itself a form of educational archaeology: hidden in common words are the original designs of education that could guide its reformation if recovered. Perrin closes by arguing that the most important educational choices we make are not our books but our colleagues—the fellow readers with whom we choose to read.
points: The word 'colleague' derives from collegere (to read together), meaning a true colleague is a fellow reader of the same books toward the same ends—not merely someone who shares an office, but someone who shares a forming intellectual project.

The original seven liberal arts were called 'liberal' because they liberate through words and numbers, and 'arts' because they make makers—of meaning, arguments, and compelling speeches; etymology reveals the original transformative purpose behind the credential category.

Assessment derives from adsedere (to sit beside): the original design of assessment was not scoring but accompaniment—coming alongside a student to help them do the next best thing, which 'correction' (from rectus, to make straight) serves.

Intelligence itself derives from intellegere (to choose among): to understand is to make wise choices—a reading of the Latin letters that must be selected and grouped to form words and meaning, connecting cognition to the act of deliberate selection.

The most important choices on any intellectual journey are the colleagues one keeps: with whom you read, discuss, and argue determines whether genuine college-in-the-original-sense continues after formal schooling ends.
quotes: A colleague, however, is more than a co-worker. Beyond possibly sharing a building, a colleague likely shares common interests, ideas, and goals. The best colleagues even share the same books.

This is retained in the old idea of a college, which is derived collegere, (and the noun collegium) which means to read together. One ideal of a college is that it would be a gathering of like-minded learners (teachers and students) who are reading the same books and for the same ends—for inquiry, study, conversation, wisdom.

They were called liberal because they liberate or set us free to understand the reality of the cosmos by means of words. Words arranged to make meaning make up grammar, words arranged to discern and display truth make up logic, words arranged to delight, instruct, and persuade make up rhetoric.

A colleague, therefore, is a fellow reader, and likely a reader of the same books, and for the same ends. This is the old ideal of a college, and a good lecture would be derived from good reading. To this day at Oxford, students does not say 'I am majoring in philosophy' but rather 'I am reading philosophy.'

Some of the most important choices we make on our intellectual journeys are our choices of colleagues. With whom you study, with whom you read, with whom you discuss and argue—what is more important? Yes, we should carefully choose our books, but with whom will we choose to read those books?
